did_you_know.text: Did you know? In this chapter, Samuel declares that he listened to the people’s request and appointed a king over them, marking the transition from Samuel’s leadership to Saul’s kingship.

Did you know? Samuel asks the people to testify whether he ever took an ox or a donkey, defrauded anyone, oppressed anyone, or accepted a bribe to overlook wrongdoing; in this way, he demonstrates his integrity and accountability as a leader.
Did you know? Samuel reminds the people that it was the Lord who brought their ancestors out of Egypt through Moses and Aaron, presenting the Exodus as a central example of the Lord’s gracious acts.
Did you know? According to Samuel’s speech, when Israel forgot the Lord, they were handed over to various enemies, including Sisera, the Philistines, and the king of Moab.
Did you know? Samuel mentions several leaders whom the Lord sent to rescue Israel: Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel. He then describes the people living securely in the land.
Did you know? The request for a king was presented as a response to their fear of Nahash, king of the Ammonites, even though the people acknowledged that the Lord was their king.
Did you know? Samuel emphasizes that Saul’s kingship does not free either the people or the king from their obligation to fear the Lord, serve him, and obey his commands.

Did you know? Samuel asks for a sign during the wheat harvest: he calls on the Lord, and thunder and rain come at that time of year to demonstrate to the people the seriousness of their request for a king.
Did you know? After the thunder and rain, the people acknowledge that by asking for a king they have added to their sins, and they ask Samuel to pray for them.
Did you know? Samuel considers ceasing to pray for the people a sin against the Lord, so he promises to continue praying for them and teaching them the good and right way.
